what_its_for: Buprenorphine is used to treat opioid use disorder (dependence on opioids like heroin or prescription pain pills). It helps reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms so you can focus on your recovery. Some forms are also used to treat moderate to severe chronic pain.
how_to_take: Buprenorphine comes in different forms. The most common form is a film or tablet that dissolves under your tongue (sublingual) or between your cheek and gum (buccal). Place the film or tablet in the correct spot and let it fully dissolve — do NOT chew, swallow, or cut it. Do not eat, drink, or smoke while it is dissolving. There is also a long-acting injection given by your doctor, and an implant placed under the skin by a healthcare provider. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for the form you are prescribed.
dosing: Your dose will be determined by your doctor based on your needs, the form of buprenorphine you are taking, and how your body responds. Doses are usually started low and slowly increased. For sublingual films or tablets, doses are typically taken once or twice a day. Never take more than prescribed — taking too much can be dangerous. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. If it is nearly time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store buprenorphine films and tablets at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it in a safe, secure location — ideally locked — away from children, teenagers, and anyone it was not prescribed for. This medication can be dangerous or deadly to someone who has not been prescribed it, especially children. If you have leftover or unused medication, dispose of it safely at a medication take-back program or a drop box near you. Do not flush unless the label says it is safe to do so.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking buprenorphine — this combination can slow your breathing and can be life-threatening. Do not take sleep aids, anti-anxiety medicines (like benzodiazepines such as Xanax or Valium), other opioids, or muscle relaxers without your doctor's approval, as combining these can cause serious breathing problems or death. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medication affects you, as it may cause drowsiness or dizziness. Do not stop taking buprenorphine suddenly without talking to your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help (911) right away if you experience: slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme drowsiness or you cannot be woken up; severe dizziness or confusion; bluish lips, fingertips, or skin; chest pain or irregular heartbeat; severe abdominal pain (which may be a sign of adrenal problems); signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you feel your medication is not controlling your cravings or withdrawal, or if you experience mood changes, worsening depression, or thoughts of self-harm.
when_it_works: Buprenorphine starts working relatively quickly. Many people feel relief from withdrawal symptoms within 1 to 3 hours of their first dose. Cravings usually become more manageable within the first few days to a week of starting treatment. However, recovery is an ongoing process, and your doctor may continue to adjust your dose over weeks or months to find what works best for you. Be patient and stay in close contact with your healthcare team.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Buprenorphine can be used during pregnancy under close medical supervision, as untreated opioid use disorder can be more harmful to you and your baby. Babies born to mothers taking buprenorphine may experience neonatal withdrawal syndrome and will need monitoring after birth. Breastfeeding: Small amounts pass into breast milk. Ask your doctor if it is safe for you to breastfeed while taking this medication. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to the effects of buprenorphine, especially dizziness and breathing problems. Use with caution and only as directed by your doctor. Liver problems: Buprenorphine is processed by your liver. Let your doctor know if you have liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted and your liver will need to be monitored.
